32.0.s.en: (1) The making of the golden calf

32.0.0.en: Moses represented the image of God to the people. So when he went up the mountain and was absent there for days, they needed a tangible image, as they had seen images of gods in Egypt. They asked Aaron for a tangible image of God to worship in place of Moses, because they doubted whether he might have died on the mountain, since he had no food or drink for the whole forty days (ch. 25:18), or whether he had lost his way in the mountain, or the divine fire had burned him. Some of them may have thought that he had been caught up to heaven like Enoch. Moses spent another forty days fasting on the mountain (ch. 34:28) to receive two new tablets of the commandments, after he broke the first two tablets when he came down from the mountain and saw the golden calf (v. 19).

32.1.0.en: Fashioned it: melted it so that it became a single mass.

32.1.1.en: Aaron yielded to the people's sinful demands. This was weakness of faith and fear on his part before the people's uprising. So he collected from them the golden earrings that were in their ears, melted them in the fire, and fashioned them with a graving tool, and he formed a calf from this gold and called it the god who brought the children of Israel out of Egypt by the ten plagues. This was a belittling of God by depicting Him as a calf, as they used to worship the calf "Apis" in Egypt or watch the Egyptians worship it. Notice the generosity of the people in giving to make the golden calf, just as we give much of our time and effort to evil. Notice also that the Holy Bible mentions the sins of the saints just as it mentions their virtues, so that we are not troubled if we fall into sin, but rise and continue our spiritual striving with God.

32.1.2.en: Hold fast to the word of God as a servant, and do not yield to the demands of those you serve in order to please them against the commandments of God, so that your only aim in every service is to draw souls to Christ.

32.2.0.en: After Aaron set up the golden calf, raised before the people, he built an altar before it and offered sacrifices on it, and they ate of them. It appears that peace offerings, part of which is burned before God on the altar while the one who offers them eats the remainder, were known among the fathers since the days of Adam. By this Aaron proclaimed a feast to the Lord Jehovah, depicted in the form of this golden calf. By making the golden calf and what they did before it, they fell into these errors:

32.2.1.en: (1) Belittling God and depicting Him as a golden calf.

32.2.2.en: (2) Offering sacrifices to this idol, which neither hears nor sees nor walks.

32.2.3.en: (3) They were absorbed in eating meat, rather than in repentance joined with offering sacrifices to God.

32.2.4.en: (4) They took part in licentious and shameless games to please their lusts, and most likely these were joined with drinking wine.

32.3.0.en: At the end of the forty days, after God finished His talk with Moses, He informed him of the evil into which the people had fallen, and commanded him to go down from the mountain to the people, who had become corrupt by making a golden calf. They offered it worship and sacrifices, and even attributed to it the power of bringing them out of the land of Egypt, and they departed far from their God. In God's distress over the people, He called them "your people," for they were no longer the people of God, because they had exchanged Him for a golden calf.

32.3.1.en: Do not lose the grace of your sonship to God, in which you enjoy a relationship of love with Him and His care, and even the eternal inheritance. Do not give up all this for any earthly lust, however pleasant or dazzling it may seem, for it is passing away and is worth nothing beside your sonship to God.

32.4.0.en: Stiff-necked: like the ox that refuses to have the yoke placed on its neck, or the horse that resists with its neck the bridle placed in its mouth. What is meant is that the people of God are obstinate like these animals. God described His people as obstinate and as refusing life with Him, and He declared to Moses that He intended to destroy this people for their wickedness and to raise up a new people from his offspring, because he had found grace in His eyes, like Noah and Abraham. We notice Moses' boldness with God, so that he even asks His permission and He says to him, "Let Me alone." For God loves His children, and they have a great place with Him. He of course knows that Moses will intercede for the people and that He will not destroy them, but He declares how wicked they are and how much they deserve, without destroying them.

32.5.0.en: Repented of the evil: ceased from taking vengeance on them.

32.5.1.en: Moses raised his prayers in humility before God, pleading for His mercies, that He would forgive His people and not destroy them, for the following reasons:

32.5.2.en: 1- Because they are the people of God, who kept them in Egypt and brought them out with great power and cares for them in the wilderness. They are His own and His children, and by this he seeks the tenderness and fatherhood of God.

32.5.3.en: 2- That He not give the Gentiles, such as the Egyptians, an opportunity to speak arrogantly against God and claim that He hates His people and brought them out with cunning in order to destroy them in the wilderness, whereas God is tender and compassionate and does not lie in His promises. That is, that He not give them an opportunity to gloat over His people.

32.5.4.en: 3- He reminds God of His promises to the fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, to give them the land of Canaan. Here the unselfishness of Moses appears: he does not think of himself and his house becoming the beginning of the people of God as Abraham did, but with fatherly love he cares for the salvation of all the people, even though they are wicked. Moses reminds God that the people are His people, so that He may have mercy on them.

32.6.0.en: The Lord repented: He turned back from His decision. It does not mean that He felt He had made a mistake, because God knows everything and does not err, but He speaks in the manner that human beings understand, namely that He is a tender Father who gave up His decision to destroy the people, agreed to Moses' intercession for his people, and abandoned His decision to destroy them. He knows what will happen and that Moses will intercede for them, but He wanted to declare what they deserve, and then, for the sake of Moses' intercession, to have mercy on them.

32.7.s.en: (3) The anger of Moses and the breaking of the tablets

32.7.0.en: On both their sides: on both faces.

32.7.1.en: Moses obeyed and went down from the mountain, departing from the presence of God, whom he saw in a certain form that may have been light or some other dazzling and wonderful form. In his hands were the two tablets of stone that God had given him, with the Ten Commandments written on both sides of each tablet. The two tablets were made by God and written by Him, and Moses alone carried them in his hands, rejoicing in their great value.

32.8.0.en: After Moses had descended some distance on the mountain, he met his disciple Joshua, who had been waiting for him for the forty days. He rejoiced at meeting him, and they went down together. When they drew near the foot of the mountain, before they saw the people, they heard the sound of their shouting, and Joshua thought it was the sound of battle, perhaps the people fighting the Amalekites, who had risen against them a second time.

32.9.1.en: Moses answered Joshua, denying his words and declaring that these sounds were not the sounds of battle, whether the voice of the victors or of the defeated, but the sound of the people singing.

32.10.0.en: Moses and Joshua continued descending from the mountain and drew near to the people, and Moses saw the golden calf raised up and the people around it dancing and singing. He became very angry at the corruption of his people in leaving God and worshiping idols, and in the intensity of his anger he cast the two tablets from him despite their great value. But he was jealous with the jealousy of a father who cares for his children when he saw them in this corruption and turning away from God.

32.11.0.en: When the people saw Moses coming quickly toward them, they were very afraid. He took the calf and threw it into the fire until it melted and became a shapeless mass, then he broke it and ground it into tiny particles and cast them into the water, and the particles floated on the surface of the water. He commanded the people to drink of it, to show them the weakness of what they had imagined to be a god, so that they would feel their sin against God when they drank, that perhaps they might repent.

32.11.1.en: Be firm with those who err, if you are responsible for your household or your work or a group of those you serve in the Church. Reject evil and remove it from the midst, keep those you serve away from it, and make them know the extent of their sin so that they may repent. But your firmness should be with fatherhood and embrace toward those you rebuke, so that they do not fall into despair or obstinacy.

32.12.0.en: Moses rebuked Aaron for yielding to the evil thoughts of the people by making a calf and calling them to worship it. By this he made them idolaters, and they disobeyed God and defied Him.

32.13.0.en: Aaron did not admit his fault but gave justifications for what he had done, which are:

32.13.1.en: (1) That the people fall into many evils, such as murmuring, as Moses knows.

32.13.2.en: (2) Moses represented the image of God to the people, so when he was absent on the mountain for a long time, they asked for a tangible image to worship.

32.13.3.en: (3) He lessened his sin by saying that he was compelled to ask them for the gold earrings and throw them into the fire, and so a calf came out, although in truth he had made an effort and used the graving tool and instruments to make a calf of gold; it did not become a calf by itself.

32.13.4.en: We notice that Aaron called Moses "my lord" although he was younger than he, out of respect for him because he was the leader of the people and the prophet of God. This speech shows the seriousness of the leader's sin, which brings punishment upon all his people, for Aaron's laxity and his yielding to the evil of his people made the people fall into the sin of idolatry.

32.14.0.en: Moses grieved when he saw a large number of the people stripped of their clothes, even if partially, and immersed in the shamelessness or licentiousness and dancing that Aaron had allowed as leader of the people, so they became a derision among their neighbors, such as the Amalekites.

32.14.1.en: Bear your responsibility, whether you are a servant, or the head of a family, or someone responsible in any place, to lead others in the way of God, and do not abandon them or encourage them in evil. For God will hold you accountable because you used your leadership and your position to keep people away from God.

32.15.0.en: The gate of the camp: the entrance to the place where they pitched their tents; perhaps they posted guards at it against an attack by the Amalekites or any of their enemies.

32.15.1.en: Who is on the Lord's side: whoever believes in God and fears Him and rejects evil.

32.15.2.en: Let him come to me: let him come toward me to help me destroy evil.

32.15.3.en: Moses stood in a visible place, which was the entrance of the place where they were dwelling, and called to the people that everyone who fears God and is zealous to please Him should gather around him. A large number of the men of the tribe of Levi, who cared for their spiritual life and their relationship with God, gathered with him.

32.16.0.en: When Moses declared the wrath of God over their worship of the calf, and had ground it, scattered it on the water and made them drink of it, many were ashamed and repented and went into their tents, but some neglected the words of Moses and persisted in their evil. Then he commanded the sons of Levi gathered around him that each one take his sword, which was placed in a sheath at the middle of each man and hung on his thigh, and pass through the tents and kill their brothers who persisted in the games of shamelessness and dancing and had stripped off their clothes. The sons of Levi obeyed the word of Moses at once and killed three thousand men of the wicked.

32.17.0.en: Consecrate yourselves (literally, fill your hands): sanctify and set apart your works for God.

32.17.1.en: Every man on his son and on his brother: by killing the wicked son or brother.

32.17.2.en: After the destruction of the evil, Moses encouraged them, saying that by this they had obeyed God and sanctified their works by destroying the wicked, even if they were their sons or their brothers, for their relationship with God is more important than emotional relationships, and by this God gives them a great blessing. Filling the hand was an expression used in the priestly work when they carry the sacrifices on their hands and offer them on the altar before God. So he called the tribe of Levi, which would be set apart for the service of God, and from which would come Aaron and his sons, to destroy the wicked, because by destroying evil they would be doing work like the priests who sanctify God, whether by offering sacrifices or by the various purifications. Here, by their destroying evil, they declare the holiness of God, who is not in agreement with evil, and please Him, and by destroying the wicked they also save the people from the spread of evil among them, so that the fear of God falls on all hearts.

32.18.0.en: On the day after the killing of the wicked, Moses showed his people how monstrous their sin was and that they deserved severe punishment, but he gave them hope that he would go up to the mountain and pray to God to ask forgiveness for their sin. This shows that many had sinned and bowed down to the calf, but they repented at Moses' call and went into their tents, and the Levites did not kill them.

32.19.0.en: Moses confessed the sin of his people before God when he returned and went up to the mountain, where he had been with God forty days. Then he interceded for them that God might forgive them, and offered himself as a ransom for his people, that he should die but the people live. Here the fatherhood of Moses appears and his readiness to lay down his life for his people as a good shepherd to them, after the pattern of Christ the Redeemer. The blotting out of his name from the book of God means his death, or not being mentioned in the Holy Bible as one of the pious. Moses was not able to redeem his people, because only Christ is able to die for His people and make atonement for them, but by these words he shows his intense love and fatherhood for his wicked people.

32.19.1.en: Pray for those around you and care for the salvation of their souls. Rather, be ready to sacrifice anything material and to bear many hardships in order to win them for Christ, remembering your Redeemer who laid down His life for you.

32.20.0.en: God rejoiced in the fatherly feelings of Moses for his people, but He showed His justice by declaring that the one who sinned is the one who bears the punishment, and if he repents God accepts him. It is not right that one person die for another, because of man's weakness and because Christ alone is able to do this in the fullness of time.

32.21.0.en: Lead the people: exhort them so that they do not return to evil and so that they repent of their sin.

32.21.1.en: The day of My visitation: the day that God appoints to punish and discipline His people so that they feel the monstrousness of their sins and keep away from them.

32.21.2.en: God asked Moses to go down from the mountain and exhort the people to an upright life. He promised him that His angel would not leave them because of their sin, but would continue to lead them in the form of the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire by day and by night, but that He would discipline them at the proper time so that they would not return to their sins. This means God's anger against them, so He deprived them of His presence in their midst and was content with the angel going before them.

32.22.0.en: God disciplined the people with plagues so that they would feel the monstrousness of idolatry. The kind of plagues is not mentioned, whether they were diseases or hunger or any other afflictions that God allowed for them, but what is mentioned is the death of three thousand of them in one day by the hand of their brothers (v. 28). Notice that His acceptance of Moses' intercession does not mean the complete removal of punishment from them but its lessening, whereas the complete removal of punishment is what is accomplished by the blood of Christ. This confirms the seriousness of sin and its consequences, which deserve many punishments, and so the love of Christ appears, which removes from us all these punishments.
